summary: Describes changes to the sockets API needed to support IPv6, including a new socket address structure, address conversion functions and some new socket options. It aims to keep applications as portable with IPv6 as they were with IPv4. It obsoletes RFC 2133 and was replaced by RFC 3493.

plainLanguage.summary: Programs use a standard plug to connect to the network. This document redesigns the plug so it fits the new, longer addresses too.

subtitle: The changes to the Berkeley sockets API that let ordinary TCP and UDP programs use 128-bit IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The sockets API exposes the size of an IP address to applications, so the 128-bit IPv6 address does not fit the existing IPv4 structures and functions.
tldr.mechanism: The memo adds a sockaddr_in6 address structure, new name lookup and address conversion functions, an IPv4-mapped address format for talking to IPv4 nodes, and a few IPV6_ socket options.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 2133, is Informational rather than a standard, and was itself obsoleted by RFC 3493 and updated by RFC 3152.

today: RFC 2553 is an Informational RFC that was obsoleted by RFC 3493, which is the one to read now. It had replaced RFC 2133 and was updated by RFC 3152.

sections.title: Goals and Design Constraints
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long and IPv6 addresses are 128 bits. The sockets API makes the address size visible to programs, so every part that exposes addresses had to change. The memo covers the basic features needed by TCP and UDP applications, including multicast. Raw sockets and access to extension headers are left to another document, RFC 2292.

The design rules are: existing programs must keep working at both source and binary level, changes should be as small as possible, programs should be able to talk to IPv6 and IPv4 hosts without knowing which, and IPv6 addresses in structures should be 64-bit aligned.

The core socket functions take opaque address pointers, so they need no change. What needs changing is the address structure, the name-to-address functions and the address conversion functions. The extensions assume a machine with full support for both IPv4 and IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: The old plug was made for short addresses. The goal is a new plug for long addresses that keeps old programs working.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Structures
sections.content:
A new AF_INET6 address family and PF_INET6 protocol family are defined. Programs create IPv6 sockets with calls such as socket(PF_INET6, SOCK_STREAM, 0).

The in6_addr structure holds one 128-bit address as sixteen 8-bit elements in network byte order. The sockaddr_in6 structure carries sin6_family, sin6_port, sin6_flowinfo (traffic class and flow label), sin6_addr and sin6_scope_id. For a link-scope address the scope id is an interface index. A variant for 4.4BSD systems adds sin6_len and an 8-bit family field, and those systems also define SIN6_LEN.

The structure is normally larger than the generic sockaddr, so code that assumes otherwise needs review. To help, the memo adds sockaddr_storage, which is big and aligned enough for any address family. Wildcard and loopback addresses are provided as in6addr_any and in6addr_loopback, plus constants IN6ADDR_ANY_INIT and IN6ADDR_LOOPBACK_INIT that may be used only when declaring a variable.
sections.plainLanguage: The address envelope gets bigger. It has room for a long address, a port, and a note saying which neighborhood the address belongs to.

sections.title: Compatibility with IPv4
sections.content:
Systems must keep supporting PF_INET sockets and sockaddr_in, and one process should be able to hold IPv4 and IPv6 sockets at the same time.

An IPv6 socket can also reach an IPv4 node through an IPv4-mapped IPv6 address. The IPv4 address goes in the low-order 32 bits and the high-order 96 bits hold the prefix 0:0:0:0:0:FFFF, written ::FFFF:<IPv4-address>. A program can connect to or send to such an address, and the system hands back mapped addresses for IPv4 peers. Few programs need to know which kind of peer they have; for those, the IN6_IS_ADDR_V4MAPPED() macro exists.
sections.plainLanguage: An old-style address can be tucked inside a new long address, like putting a short street number after a long fixed prefix. That lets one new program talk to both old and new neighbors.

sections.title: Interface Indexes and Socket Options
sections.content:
Interfaces are identified by an interface index, a small positive integer starting at 1 (0 is never used). Four functions map names and indexes: if_nametoindex(), if_indextoname(), if_nameindex() and if_freenameindex().

New socket options all use level IPPROTO_IPV6. IPV6_UNICAST_HOPS sets the hop limit: -1 means the kernel default, 0 to 255 is used as given, and other values give EINVAL. Sending multicast is controlled by IPV6_MULTICAST_IF, IPV6_MULTICAST_HOPS and IPV6_MULTICAST_LOOP; the multicast hop limit defaults to 1 and loopback defaults to on. Receiving uses IPV6_JOIN_GROUP and IPV6_LEAVE_GROUP with an ipv6_mreq structure. To receive multicast datagrams, a process must join the group and bind the UDP port.
sections.plainLanguage: Each network connection on your computer gets a number. Options are small switches, such as how far a message may travel and which groups you listen to.

sections.title: Name and Address Functions
sections.content:
Because gethostbyname() is not thread safe and cannot say which address types are wanted, the memo adds the thread-safe getipnodebyname() and getipnodebyaddr(), with freehostent() to release results. A flags value of 0 is strict: AF_INET returns only IPv4 and AF_INET6 only IPv6. The flag AI_DEFAULT combines AI_V4MAPPED and AI_ADDRCONFIG and suits most programs.

For protocol-independent lookups it describes getaddrinfo(), taken from a POSIX draft, which turns a node name and service name into a linked list of addrinfo structures ready for socket(), bind() or connect(). The reverse is getnameinfo(), with NI_MAXHOST of 1025 and NI_MAXSERV of 32.

For converting text and binary forms, inet_pton() and inet_ntop() replace the IPv4-only functions and work for both families. INET_ADDRSTRLEN is 16 and INET6_ADDRSTRLEN is 46. Macros such as IN6_IS_ADDR_LOOPBACK and IN6_IS_ADDR_MULTICAST test for special addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: These are phone-book helpers. You give a name and get back the address to call, or give an address and get back the name, and they work for both the old and the new kinds of numbers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says only a little here. IPv6 provides a number of new security mechanisms, many of which need to be accessible to applications, and companion memos about socket extensions for IPv6 security were still being written. This document does not define those extensions itself.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 has new safety features that programs will want to use. This document does not cover them and says other papers will.
